newsitem.title: SPAIN: Matador issuance could slow, but specials seen.
newsitem.headline: Matador issuance could slow, but specials seen.

text.p: Spain's peseta eurobond market, which blossomed in 1996, could face a tough 1997 as investors adopt a less aggressive approach toward fixed-income assets.
Structured deals, such as index-linked bonds or issues with options, should keep some investors' appetite piqued.
But overall issuance is expected to fall this year after the amount of matadors issued almost tripled in 1996 from 1995, achieving a volume equal to that of the prior three years together.

"With such a low level in interest rates, I expect less buying interest this year than in the previous one. But, still I expect a busy 1997," said Ignacio Miranda, director of capital markets at Banco Central Hispano in Madrid.
The Matador primary market in 1996 saw new issues for 859.3 billion pesetas, up from 318 billion pesetas in 1995.
"We can't expect to have another year like 1996 when our activity was the same as we saw in 1993, 1994 and 1995 together," said Emilio De Las Heras of Argentaria Capital Markets.
"This year, I would expect something like 500 or 600 billion pesetas," he said.

The more sophisticated segment of Spanish domestic investors eager for higher returns than those offered by government bonds will be enticed by index-linked yield or callable options, while traditional Matador clients, such as retail investors in Luxembourg and in central Europe, remain more interested in shorter-term maturities, Miranda said.
"With these structured deals, domestic investors can have a spread over the T-bond," Miranda said.
And this can be of special importance when yields are at a record low level.
"Instead of being sure of getting almost nothing, people prefer taking the risk," said De Las Heras.

The sharp reduction in yields after the market began to believe Spain might get fit for Europe's single currency from the start in 1999 "has created room for Matadors also because it had reduced the domestic borrowers demand," a dealer said.

The March long-term future ended the year at 112.80 after starting on January 2, 1996 at 96.38. In the cash market, the 10-year spread over German Bunds declined from 330 basis points in March to 100 basis points, currently.
The European Investment Bank, the biggest 1996 borrower in the Matador market, was also the first to get going this year.
On January 7, it launched a six-tranche equity-linked bond with different maturities for a total 36.083 billion pesetas.
"A likely more volatile market this year will favour further structured issues," echoed Luis Ordonez, dealer at Banco Santander de Negocios in Madrid.
And today, the International Finance Corporation issued a six-tranche equity-linked Ibex-35 bond for a total of 5.745 billion pesetas.
